slides.title: What is Reverse Beamforming?
slides.notes: Ask first, then click through. Beamforming steers what an antenna array sends; reverse beamforming listens with the array and computes the direction of arrival from the arrival-time (phase) differences. BLEARVIS (IMWUT 2023) mounts such an array on the headset and fuses the angle of arrival of BLE tags with camera-based object detection.

r.t: : several antennas send the same signal, each a little later than its neighbour. The waves add up in one direction (5G, Wi-Fi).

slides.title: Will AI Replace Software Engineers?

items.alt: Newspaper clipping, The Lexington Leader, 27 October 1960: "IBM Experts Say Electronic Brains Offer No Threat To Taking Over Man's World"

slides.notes: The fear that machines take over our work is older than the computer industry. In 1960, IBM experts had to reassure the public. Ask the room: what has happened to programming jobs since?

slides.title: 80 Years of Programming: **A Quick Run-Through**

r.t: “Planners” design, “coders” translate into instructions by hand.
Software becomes an engineering discipline: teams, tests, processes.
Reuse instead of rewriting: GitHub, Stack Overflow, libraries.
From autocomplete to agents that complete whole tasks on their own.
Humans describe more and more of the What. Machines take over more and more of the How.

slides.notes: What does a human have to write down to add two numbers or to solve a task? 1945: plug cables. 1950s: machine instructions, with a division of labour: planners (often mathematicians) designed the program, coders translated it by hand. 1957, FORTRAN: the compiler takes over the translation. 1968: the NATO conference in Garmisch coins the term software engineering, because software had grown too large to manage (software crisis). 2000s: we write less ourselves and assemble more. Since 2022: we describe in natural language what we want. Each step moves the work from the How to the What.

slides.title: **The Compiler**: Automating Programming in the 1950s

r.t: Nobody believed that. I had a running compiler and nobody would touch it.
They told me computers could only do arithmetic.
The machine took over the work of the “coders”: turning plans into machine instructions by hand.
Software became cheaper, so much more software was built. More programmers were needed, not fewer.
Understanding, specifying, designing, testing: humans state the What, the machine does the How.

items.alt: Grace Hopper in her navy uniform at a desk with a computer terminal, raising one finger

slides.notes: Grace Hopper built one of the first compilers in 1952. The reaction was scepticism: a computer cannot produce programs by itself. Sounds familiar? What happened next: the coders' work, translating by hand, was automated. The profession did not disappear: cheaper software meant much more software. And human work moved up to understanding, specifying, designing and testing. The quote is widely reported, e.g. in Billings, "Grace Hopper: Navy Admiral and Computer Pioneer".

slides.title: What Do Software Engineers Do Today?

r.t: Clarify the problem, the users and the constraints
Define what exactly the system should do
Integrate, release, maintain, and answer for it
Software projects are highly complex socio-technical artefacts

slides.notes: Writing code (red) is only one link in the chain. Before it: understanding what is needed, specifying it precisely, designing. After it: verifying, integrating, releasing, operating, and taking responsibility when something goes wrong.

slides.title: The Decide-Execute-Deliver Sandwich

items.alt: A tall burger with three patties and tomatoes on a plate

r.t: What to build: requirements, priorities, trade-offs
Review, integrate, release, operate, take responsibility

slides.source: Narayanan & Kapoor: [Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t](https://www.normaltech.ai/p/why-ai-hasnt-replaced-software-engineers), AI as Normal Technology, 2026. Burger image: AI-generated
slides.notes: Narayanan and Kapoor describe knowledge work as a decide-execute-deliver sandwich. AI compresses the middle layer; the other two layers depend on human judgement and responsibility.

slides.title: The Compiler Already Squeezed the Sandwich Once

r.t: Execute dominates: every line is translated into machine instructions by hand.
Execute shrinks. Software gets cheaper, and much more of it is built.
Execute shrinks again. Deciding and delivering become the bottleneck.

slides.notes: The compiler did the same: it squeezed the middle layer, and there are more software engineers today than ever, because cheaper software creates more demand. With AI, Execute gets much thinner again. The layer heights are schematic, not measured. Deliver is drawn larger on the right; the next slides show why.
slides.source: Schematic, after Narayanan & Kapoor (2026), AI as Normal Technology

slides.title: What Remains When Writing Code Gets Cheap?

r.t: The hardest single part of building a software system is
Syntax, memory, boilerplate: how do I tell the machine?
→ Shrinks with every tool: compilers, IDEs, libraries, AI
Requirements, trade-offs, special cases: what should the system actually do?
→ Remains, and grows with the size of the systems

slides.notes: Brooks separates accidental complexity (how to tell the machine) from essential complexity (what the system should do). Every tool so far has reduced the accidental part. Architectural trade-offs, the topic of the second half of this course, are essential complexity.

slides.title: Like the Compiler, and Yet Different

r.t: Humans describe the goal, the machine generates the code.
“Computers cannot write programs”, in 1952 as today.
Cheaper software → more software, not less work.
Nobody reads compiler output, because it is generated deterministically. AI output must be checked, at least indirectly.
Prompts are ambiguous, like natural-language specifications.
Three generations of tools since 2021: autocomplete, agents, autonomous agents.
So the work does not disappear. It moves to verifying and delivering.

slides.notes: Much is the same as with the compiler. One point is fundamentally different: a compiler is deterministic and formally specified, so nobody reads the machine code it produces. An AI model is probabilistic: the same prompt can give different results, and they can be wrong, so a human must check. Prompts are natural language and therefore ambiguous. And the pace is unprecedented. Consequence: Execute gets thinner, Deliver becomes the bottleneck. Can this be measured?

slides.title: More Code = More Software? Not So Simple

items.alt: Bar chart on a log scale: after adopting AI coding tools, developers write 25.5 times as many lines of code, 5.0 times as many files, 3.4 times as many commits, 2.7 times as many pull requests, 1.8 times as many projects, but only 1.3 times as many releases.

r.t: The closer to delivery, the smaller the effect.
69% of new repositories see no activity after their first month (2021: 60%).

slides.notes: The production chain of software from left to right: lines of code, files, commits, pull requests, projects, releases. Log scale. With all three tool generations, developers write about 25 times as many lines, but release only about 1.3 times as much. The effect weakens at every step that needs a human: review, integration, release. Sync agents alone: +958% lines of code, +86% pull requests, +20% releases. More projects are started and abandoned: the share of new repositories without activity after the first month rose from 60% (2021) to 69%.
slides.source: Cumulative effect of three generations of AI tools, log scale. Demirer, Musolff & Yang: [Writing Code vs. Shipping Code](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35275), NBER Working Paper 35275, 2026, Fig. 1
